name: Auditory pathway
summary: Hair cells of the organ of Corti excite spiral ganglion neurons whose axons form the cochlear nerve to the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei. From there the pathway becomes bilateral almost immediately: fibers cross in the trapezoid body to the contralateral superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus, others ascend ipsilaterally, and further crossings occur at the inferior colliculus. All fibers relay in the inferior colliculus, then the medial geniculate body, and reach Heschl's gyrus through the acoustic radiation. The extensive crossing means a unilateral central lesion never causes deafness; unilateral deafness is always the cochlea, nerve or cochlear nuclei.

origin.note: Inner hair cells of the cochlea; bipolar spiral ganglion neurons.

neuronChain.synapse: superior olivary complex (both sides) and inferior colliculus via the lateral lemniscus
medial geniculate body via its brachium
Heschl's gyrus via the acoustic radiation

decussation.level: Trapezoid body (caudal pons), lateral lemniscus commissure, inferior colliculus commissure
decussation.note: Multiple partial crossings; the pathway is bilateral above the cochlear nuclei.

waypoints.note: at the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle
acoustic radiation in the sublenticular capsule

termination: Primary auditory cortex on Heschl's gyrus, tonotopically organized, with onward projection to the auditory association cortex and Wernicke's area.

lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Ipsilateral sensorineural deafness (noise, ototoxicity, presbycusis, Ménière)
Ipsilateral deafness with poor speech discrimination and tinnitus (schwannoma, AICA infarct)

lesionEffectsByLevel.level: Superior olive, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus
lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Impaired sound localization and central auditory processing without deafness
Cortical deafness or pure word deafness

pearls: Deafness in one ear is peripheral; the brainstem and cortex cannot deafen a single ear
Brainstem auditory evoked potentials track the pathway wave by wave: I nerve, II cochlear nucleus, III superior olive, IV lateral lemniscus, V inferior colliculus

somatotopy: Tonotopic at every level: high frequencies at the base of the cochlea and in the ventral cochlear nucleus, mapped systematically through the colliculus and geniculate to Heschl's gyrus (low frequencies anterolateral, high posteromedial).
